title: Conflict and war
note: Latin bellum, war, gives bellicose and belligerent; casus belli is the event that justifies a war. A Pyrrhic victory, named for King Pyrrhus, whose wins against Rome cost him troops he could not replace, is a win so costly it amounts to defeat. Internecine first meant deadly or mutually destructive and now usually means conflict within a group.

items.a: involving conflict within a group
items.ex: Internecine feuds split the party just before the election.

items.a: a nation or group engaged in war
items.ex: Both belligerents agreed to let aid convoys through.

items.a: eager to fight; warlike
items.ex: The general's bellicose speeches alarmed the neighboring states.

items.a: a long-standing rival or agent of downfall
items.ex: The quarterback finally beat his old nemesis in the title game.

items.a: to stir up trouble or rebellion
items.ex: Agents were sent to foment unrest in the border towns.

items.a: a noisy disturbance or quarrel
items.ex: A fracas broke out in the stands after the disputed goal.

items.a: a complicated and embarrassing dispute or situation
items.ex: The seating chart became a family imbroglio that lasted until the wedding.

items.a: a prolonged bitter feud, often seeking revenge
items.ex: The two families carried on a vendetta for three generations.

items.a: a restoration of friendly relations
items.ex: The ping-pong tour helped spark a rapprochement between the two countries.

items.a: an easing of tension between rival states
items.ex: The arms treaties of the 1970s marked a period of détente.

items.a: an agreement to stop fighting
items.ex: The armistice of November 11, 1918, ended the fighting on the Western Front.

items.a: to surrender, usually on agreed terms
items.ex: After a six-month siege, the city capitulated.

items.a: a decisive defeat that causes disorderly retreat
items.ex: The game was a rout: 42 to 3 at halftime.

items.a: to defeat thoroughly
items.ex: The champion vanquished every challenger that season.

items.a: to put an end to, especially by force
items.ex: Troops were sent to quell the riot.

items.a: to bring under domination or control
items.ex: The empire subjugated its neighbors one by one.

items.a: intended to end hostility or win goodwill
items.ex: Her conciliatory letter opened the door to new talks.

items.a: to soothe someone's anger or anxiety
items.ex: A free dessert mollified the diners who had waited an hour.

items.a: to win or regain the favor of; to appease
items.ex: Ancient sailors offered sacrifices to propitiate the sea gods.

items.a: a state of deep mutual hostility
items.ex: The old enmity between the towns dated to a stolen church bell.

items.a: an act or event used to justify a war
d: a policy of recovering lost land
items.ex: The sinking of the ship became the casus belli.

items.a: a victory won at too great a cost
d: a defeat that ends a war
items.ex: Winning the lawsuit after ten years of fees was a Pyrrhic victory.

items.a: a gradual wearing down through sustained pressure
items.ex: The trench war became a war of attrition.

items.a: a sudden invasion or raid into territory
items.ex: Border guards reported an incursion at dawn.

items.a: an attack by troops coming out of a defensive position
items.ex: The besieged garrison made a night sortie to burn the enemy's ladders.

items.a: a rapid series of shots, or a barrage of criticism
items.ex: The minister faced a fusillade of questions about the contract.

items.a: a stronghold of a principle or activity
d: a weak point in a defense
items.ex: The small paper was a bastion of independent reporting.

items.a: pushing a crisis to the edge of disaster to win
items.ex: The budget standoff was brinkmanship, with a shutdown hours away.

items.a: a policy of seeking to regain lost territory
items.ex: Historians trace the war partly to revanchism over a lost province.

items.a: a display of military threat
items.ex: Naval exercises off the coast were seen as saber-rattling.
